anchors.paper_title: Neocortical and Hippocampal Theta Oscillations Track Audiovisual Integration and Replay of Speech Memories
anchors.reason: The candidate paper title and abstract directly match the dataset's topic and authors, describing the specific study that generated the raw MEG data.

metadata.methods_description: MEG data were collected during a single session per participant using continuous recording split into five runs. The experimental paradigm consisted of repeated blocks with three successive tasks: (1) encoding phase with audiovisual speech movies (5 s) and synchrony detection responses, (2) distractor phase with odd/even number judgments (20 trials), and (3) retrieval phase with visual speaker cues (5 s) followed by two-alternative forced choice between matching and non-matching auditory speech stimuli. Anatomical T1-weighted MRI scans were acquired for some participants.

citation_details.title: A large-scale heterogeneous 3D magnetic resonance brain imaging dataset for self-supervised learning
citation_details.author: Asbjørn Munk, Stefano Cerri, Jakob Ambsdorf, Julia Machnio, S. Llambias, V. Nersesjan, C. H. Krag, Peirong Liu, Pablo Rocamora-García, Mostafa Mehdipour-Ghazi, Mikael Boesen, M. Benros, J. E. Iglesias, Mads Nielsen
citation_details.abstract: We present FOMO260K, a large-scale, heterogeneous dataset of 260,927 brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans from 77,589 MRI sessions and 55,378 subjects, aggregated from 910 publicly available sources. The dataset includes both clinical- and research-grade images, multiple MRI sequences, and a wide range of anatomical and pathological variability, including scans with large brain anomalies. Minimal preprocessing was applied to preserve the original image characteristics while reducing entry barriers for new users. Companion code for self-supervised pretraining and finetuning is provided, along with pretrained models. FOMO260K is intended to support the development and benchmarking of self-supervised learning methods in medical imaging at scale.

citation_details.title: Pre-stimulus alpha power modulates trial-by-trial variability in theta rhythmic multisensory entrainment strength and theta-induced memory effect
citation_details.author: Danying Wang, Eleonora Marcantoni, Kimron L. Shapiro, Simon Hanslmayr
citation_details.abstract: Abstract Binding multisensory information into episodic memory depends partly on the timing of the hippocampal theta rhythm which provides time windows for synaptic modification. In humans, theta rhythmic sensory stimulation (RSS) enhances episodic memory when the stimuli are synchronised across the visual and auditory domain compared to when they are out-of-synchrony. However, recent studies show mixed evidence if the improvement in episodic memory is the result of modulating hippocampal theta activity. In the current study, we investigated whether pre-stimulus brain state could explain part of this variance in the neural and behavioural effects induced by the RSS, via recording participants’ brain activity with MEG during a multisensory theta RSS memory paradigm. Our findings suggest that pre-stimulus alpha power modulates entrainment strength in sensory regions, which in turn predicts subsequent memory formation. citation_details.title: Non-invasive tracking of hippocampal theta oscillations
citation_details.author: E. Marcantoni, Christoph Daube, D. Wang, C. Cao, B. Su, S. Zhan, R. A. A. Ince, Lauri Parkkonen, Satu Palva, D. Bush, Simon Hanslmayr
citation_details.abstract: Abstract Hippocampal theta oscillations play a crucial role in the formation of episodic memories by binding multisensory information into coherent episodes. Brain stimulation studies suggest that memory performance can be modulated by targeting these oscillations, offering a potential way of treating memory disorders. However, to effectively engage these rhythms, precise knowledge about their presence, frequency, phase and location is required, which has been a challenge, particularly for non-invasive methods such as magnetoencephalography (MEG). Here, we first asked if hippocampal signals are detectable in MEG recordings. Using simultaneous MEG-intracranial EEG (iEEG) data, we show that invasively recorded hippocampal activity is reflected in MEG sensor signals, demonstrating the feasibility of detecting deep-brain activity non-invasively. citation_details.title: Neocortical and Hippocampal Theta Oscillations Track Audiovisual Integration and Replay of Speech Memories
citation_details.author: Biau E, Wang D, Park H, Jensen O, Hanslmayr S
citation_details.abstract: This dataset contains raw MEG recordings, anatomical T1-weighted MRI scans, and behavioral data from an audiovisual speech memory study. Participants performed a three-phase task involving encoding of audiovisual speech movies with synchrony judgments, a distractor task, and retrieval of speech memories cued by speaker faces. The study investigates how neocortical and hippocampal theta oscillations support audiovisual integration and memory replay of speech information.

citation_details.title: THE EMERGENCE OF THE MODERN HUMAN MIND: INNER SPEECH AND ITS LINK TO MEMORY MECHANISMS
citation_details.author: Francisco Aboitiz, Javiera Parada-Palma, Florencia Álamos-Grau, Rodrigo Henríquez-Ch
citation_details.abstract: Inner speech (IS) is considered a unique feature of the human brain and an important component of mental life in many individuals, although it is not uniformly experienced across people.. The dysregulation of IS, in terms of its frequency, contents, or self-monitoring, has been linked to distinct neuropsychiatric conditions. In the child, more complex forms of IS usually develop around 7 years of age, when language is already well developed. While this phenomenon has usually been attributed to the maturation of verbal working memory circuits, this view does not account for the rich mental experiences and remembrances that accompany this phenomenon, which were highlighted by Lev Vygotsky's foundational studies. citation_details.title: Assessing the longevity of the Theta-induced Memory Effect (TIME)
citation_details.author: E. Marcantoni, Danying Wang, Kimron L. Shapiro, S. Hanslmayr
citation_details.abstract: Theta-phase synchronisation between visual and auditory rhythmically modulated sensory stimuli during encoding has been shown to enhance associative memory, an effect known as Theta-Induced Memory Effect (TIME). However, whether this advantage is short-lived or persists over time remains unknown. To address this, we examined the TIME effect in 52 participants randomly assigned to a short-delay group (immediate retrieval) or a long-delay group (retrieval after 24 hours). Electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded during incidental encoding of audio-video pairs. The luminance of the video clips and the amplitude of the sounds were modulated at theta frequency (4 Hz) and presented either in-synchrony (0° phase offset between audio and video) or out-of-synchrony (the sound 180° phase-shifted relative to the video). citation_details.title: Semantic elaboration determines the time course of alpha-beta oscillations during the encoding and retrieval of narrative memories
citation_details.author: Emmanuel Biau, Francesca M. Branzi
citation_details.abstract: Understanding and remembering everyday events requires us to retrieve semantic relationships between elements by activating prior knowledge, allowing us to form a deeper memory trace. However, the neural interplay between semantic and episodic systems to encode and retrieve recent memories remains unclear. The present study addresses how semantic elaboration enhances episodic memory formation through neural oscillations. We presented participants with continuous auditory verbal and non-verbal narratives to memorise. Participants rated the perceived coherence of each narrative to provide a subjective measure of semantic elaboration.
